Jim Rogers on crossing territory where people don't always make it home, and the street-level logic that kept him alive. His read: you don't need to know the threat. You need to read the room. → Locals telegraph danger before it arrives — watch them, not the horizon → Excitement and apprehension live in the same moment → "It'll be fine" is a thought, not a plan → Survival is awareness stacked on decisions → If you come back, use the moment to reset what matters What's a risk that taught you to pay closer attention?

Jim Rogers has drove through US and across Canada multiple times. He says it changed how he sees the world, not because of the data, but because of the exposure. Different regions, different economies, different ways of thinking about North America, all compressed into one country. I've lived this. Growing up in an immigrant family in Ontario, then working inside IBM, Motorola, Ministry of Transportation Ontario, and JP Morgan. Moving from the Caribbean to Canada then the USA, Europe and then coming back to Canada to grow some roots. Every shift in geography forced a shift in perspective. You see people's attitude towards work and life in Norway vs North Carolina. I used to go on jogs in Copehagen and walk to work long enough that the unfamiliarity becomes insight. So many of them.

Stop listening to others! Pursue what you love! Forget the haters. Your happiness is what counts most. Be the gardener, be the artist, whatever makes you smile! • Love gardening? Go for it! 🌱 • Success = happiness + passion. • Ignore the haters; follow your heart! What’s your passion? Let me know!

Your small town is not your limit. Your mindset is.** This guy grew up in the backwoods of Alabama. When he went to Yale, his phone number was five. Not 555-1234. Five. He did not know how to use a dial telephone. At Yale, he learned how to use one. He said nobody there had heard of him. Nobody knew his town. Nobody cared where he came from. And that changed his life. He went from a place where few people thought big… To rooms filled with new ideas, new standards, new expectations. Later, he studied at Oxford. New country. New people. New ways of thinking. That exposure shaped him. Here is the lesson: • Your starting point does not decide your future. • New environments force growth. • New people expand your thinking. • Skills you lack today mean nothing long term. He did not walk in prepared. He walked in willing. How often do you avoid rooms where you feel behind? How often do you stay where you feel comfortable? Growth comes from being the least experienced person in the room. Put yourself in bigger rooms. Learn what you do not know. Let new standards raise yours. Follow for more stories like this.

The first guest on Pale Blue Nexus co-founded the Quantum Fund with George Soros, predicted the commodities boom before anyone saw it coming, and moved his entire family to Singapore because he bet on Asia's century. Jim Rogers sat down with us and said something I can't stop thinking about. He's built and lost fortunes. Traveled the world twice, once by motorcycle, once by a 1 of 1 Mercedes. And when I asked him what actually separates the people who make it from the people who don't, his answer had nothing to do with markets.
